generatedProse.concept-context: Academic work in any subject swings between the two modes all the time. Planning a piece of work starts divergent: you set down the many ways a question could be approached, including awkward ones. Then it turns convergent: you weigh those options against what is feasible and sound, and choose. Running both at once, judging each idea as it arrives, tends to leave you with the first safe option and little else.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students planning the same essay, with twenty minutes before a seminar.

Student A picks an argument straight away and starts writing, judging each sentence as it comes. Twenty minutes later only half a paragraph exists, each line reworked twice. Student A ran both modes at once, generating and judging in the same breath, so little was produced and less survived.

Student B spends the first ten minutes listing every angle on the question, good and bad, without stopping to judge. Then, in the second ten, they read the list, cross out the weak ones, and pick the two that connect into an argument. Generating first and choosing second gave them more to work with, and a stronger choice.

Both had the same twenty minutes. Only Student B kept the two modes apart, which let the ideas flow and then settle.
generatedProse.summary: In any subject, creative thinking uses two modes: divergent thinking generates possibilities, and convergent thinking narrows them to the strongest. You can now tell the two apart, see why generating should come before judging, and choose the mode that fits the stage you are at. The next lesson looks at the barriers that stop this working, and how to move past them.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B do that let the ideas flow?

items.text: They generated a list of angles first, without judging, then chose afterwards.
They started writing the argument straight away and judged each line.
They spent the whole time polishing one sentence.
They waited for a single good idea to arrive.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B generated first and judged second, keeping the two modes apart.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that separated generating from judging.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The ideas flowed because Student B generated a list first and judged afterwards. Writing straight away, polishing one line, or waiting for one idea all collapse the two modes together.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
